question: Does a tutorial that combines automatic differentiation, conic/Fenchel duality, first-order primal-dual algorithms, and modern software provide a sound and reproducible route from classical optimization programs to scalable, end-to-end learned optimization pipelines?

key_findings.claim: Author scope: this is a tutorial synthesis with a running NNLS example, not a new learned optimizer or a comparative algorithmic contribution.
key_findings.evidence: The stated contribution is to unify differentiable programming, cone programming, Lagrangian/Fenchel-Rockafellar duality, PDG/ADMM/PDHG, software packages, and six application sketches. Most update rules and frameworks are established methods, and the only trained object in a detailed end-to-end example is a small sensing matrix rather than an optimizer policy that generalizes across instances.

key_findings.claim: Author tutorial result: reverse-mode automatic differentiation can be read as the adjoint solution of a Lagrangian-constrained computation graph.
key_findings.evidence: For the unconstrained part of NNLS, the graph z=Ax, y=z-b, f=||y||^2/2 gives the familiar gradient A^T(Ax-b). Introducing multipliers for the intermediate equalities yields a triangular stationarity system whose back-substitution gives the same gradient. This is a correct pedagogical example, explicitly setting aside x>=0.

key_findings.claim: Author survey: PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow, TVM, CVXPYLayers, PyEPO, and Deep Declarative Networks cover complementary execution and differentiation layers.
key_findings.evidence: The paper distinguishes dynamic/function-transformed/dataflow autodiff frameworks and compiler lowering from optimization-specific packages. It describes CVXPYLayers' DPP and implicit cone-program differentiation, PyEPO's surrogate gradients for discrete predict-then-optimize problems, and DDNs' optimality-system Jacobian-vector products.

key_findings.claim: Author method: constrained convex programs can be exposed to differentiable frameworks through penalties, null-space parameterization, dual reformulation, unrolling, or implicit differentiation, each with distinct assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: Equality penalties only approach feasibility as their weight grows; null-space reduction assumes full row rank and still must handle nonnegativity; conjugate dual optimization needs a tractable differentiable f* and strong-duality regularity. Unrolling stores solver history, whereas implicit differentiation needs a differentiable, nonsingular local optimality system and solves a linear system in the backward pass.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the Fenchel-Rockafellar NNLS derivation drops the dual-feasibility constraint and therefore does not agree with the Lagrangian dual as claimed.
key_findings.evidence: In Equation (33), inf_{x>=0} y^T A x equals zero only when A^T y>=0 and is -infinity otherwise. The paper discards this condition and prints max_y -||y||^2/2-b^T y. For the scalar instance A=b=1, its unconstrained expression has value 1/2 at y=-1 while the primal optimum is 0; adding y>=0 restores value 0. The later Equation (77) correctly includes the equivalent sign-convention constraint, confirming the omission.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the displayed generic PDHG dual has the wrong sign on F*.
key_findings.evidence: For min_x F(Kx)+G(x), Fenchel duality gives max_y -G*(-K*y)-F*(y). Equation (49) instead prints max_y -(G*(-K*y)-F*(y)), which expands to -G*(-K*y)+F*(y). The subsequent saddle form and NNLS example use the correct minus-F* structure, so the generic formula is internally inconsistent.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the purported PDG treatment of NNLS both projects and dualizes the same nonnegativity constraint, and its claimed KKT convergence fails even on a scalar example.
key_findings.evidence: The Lagrangian uses -mu^T x with mu>=0, but Equation (41) also projects x>=0. Then mu_{k+1}=[mu_k-sigma x_{k+1}]_+ can never grow from zero. With A=1 and b=-1, x*=0 needs multiplier mu*=1 for stationarity; initialized at x=mu=0, the printed iteration stays at (0,0), which is primal-optimal but violates stationarity. One must either optimize x over R and dualize the inequality or project x without this multiplier.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the ADMM and PDHG presentation suppresses conditions needed for the blanket convergence language.
key_findings.evidence: The paper presents standard NNLS ADMM and primal-first PDHG updates, but Algorithm 2 does not state the usual step-size restriction tied to ||K||, and the ADMM claim omits solvability and regularity qualifications. Figure 3 is one unidentified synthetic trajectory with no dimensions, data distribution, step sizes, or uncertainty, so it illustrates rather than validates comparative convergence.

key_findings.claim: Author distinction: implicit differentiation is solver-agnostic only locally and conditionally, not a universal gradient through arbitrary optima.
key_findings.evidence: Equation (60) requires continuous differentiability and nonsingular D_z F. For optimization layers the text additionally names strong duality, active-set nondegeneracy, and a nonsingular KKT Jacobian. Degenerate, nonunique, nonsmooth, or active-set-changing solutions can violate differentiability, a boundary not revisited in the case-study claims.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the printed PyTorch NNLS programs are not self-contained reproducible implementations.
key_findings.evidence: The ADMM snippet calls recover_x_from_mu_active_set with undefined tau and max_refine; the saddle-learning snippet additionally uses undefined r_KKT, tau, max_refine, and the recovery routine. The distributed snippet again invokes an unspecified active-set recovery. The code illustrates tensor operations, but cannot run as printed and does not establish its scalability claims.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: optimizing per-instance primal/dual variables with Adam is labeled 'learning' but demonstrates no learned optimizer or cross-instance generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Equations (67) and the code minimize over lambda,mu while maximizing over z for one fixed NNLS instance; this is a classical saddle solver implemented with autodiff. Figure 6 repeats it at five small dimensions but reports iteration trajectories only. No model maps problem data to updates or solutions, no training/test instance split exists, and no learned rule is compared out of distribution.

key_findings.claim: Author toy result: a CVXPYLayer can backpropagate through NNLS to fit a sensing matrix, but the demonstration is a non-identifiable single-example inverse fit.
key_findings.evidence: For one 6-by-4 sensing setup, Adam updates P for 300 steps until reconstruction loss reaches 2.8e-16 and KKT residuals are around 1e-4. Many matrices can make a single x_true optimal for its b, so this shows gradient plumbing and memorization, not recovery of P_true, generalization to new signals, or a better optimization algorithm.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the empirical scale is far below the 'massive-scale' framing and lacks basic protocol reporting.
key_findings.evidence: The backprop NNLS reaches only m=150,n=100; the Stigler scalability plot stops at 200-by-500 and shows a CVXPY/Clarabel curve; the signal example is 6-by-4; the wireless example has four links and two constraints; the LR-NNLS check is 50-by-30. Seeds, instance-generation distributions, hardware, wall-time methodology, solver tolerances, and error bars are not reported.

key_findings.claim: Author case-study boundary: the lossless-convexification sketch is exact only under external regularity conditions that are not stated or tested in the tutorial instance.
key_findings.evidence: The relaxation replaces the nonconvex lower thrust norm by Gamma and asserts Gamma*=||u*|| under 'suitable regularity conditions,' referring readers to prior work. No numerical table, actual dynamics Gz=h, parameter values, gradient task, or counterexample is supplied in the reviewed PDF despite a sentence saying numerical results validate the property.

anchors.section: NOCP-Relaxed, NOCP-Dual, and claimed numerical validation

key_findings.claim: Author case-study result: the conditional Perron-Frobenius rate-domain reformulation supports a differentiable four-link wireless example.
key_findings.evidence: Under irreducibility and nonnegativity of each quasi-inverse matrix, the rate region becomes log-rho(B_tilde diag(exp r))<=0 and admits exponential-cone modeling. Figure 12 shows CVXPY/CVXPYLayers agreement, recovered powers, one active spectral constraint, and the envelope gradient dV*/dw=r*. The result is conditional and tiny, not evidence for arbitrary NP-hard sum-rate instances.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the OPF 'dual' invokes an inverse square root of the graph Laplacian that the paper itself defines as singular, and the proposed PDG has no global guarantee for the nonconvex problem.
key_findings.evidence: G is introduced as a weighted Laplacian, hence G1=0, yet OPF-Dual contains G^{-1/2}; this is undefined without a restricted subspace or pseudoinverse. Its displayed PSD product is not shown symmetric. The method then ignores voltage bounds in the dual derivation, reinstates them by projection, retains quadratic nonconvex power constraints, and offers no convexity, constraint qualification, convergence theorem, or numerical OPF result. Table 2's 'global optimal solution' benefit is therefore unsupported by this section.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the LRMP primal-recovery formula assumes a connected graph and its numerical 'recovery' is circular.
key_findings.evidence: From L1=0 the paper jumps to x*=-L^dagger g+c1, but a disconnected graph has a higher-dimensional null space, and solvability also requires g in range(L). For constrained LR-NNLS it says scalar c is uniquely determined, then estimates c using the already-known CVXPY primal x* in c=(1/n)1^T(x*-z). An error near 1e-6 therefore checks a fitted decomposition using the target solution; it does not recover x* from dual variables alone.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the artifact carries impossible placeholder publication metadata and demonstrably unrelated citations.
key_findings.evidence: The v4 PDF dated July 2026 calls itself J. ACM 37(4), August 2018 with an XXXXXXX DOI, then ends 'Received 20 February 2007; revised 12 March 2009; accepted 5 June 2009.' Reference 68 on Lagrangian/Legendrian symplectic invariants is cited for optimization duality, and reference 187, a paper on political leaning from tweets, is cited as an LRMP source. These are not cosmetic typos when assessing version-of-record status and scholarly support.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the conclusion overstates adaptive, accelerated, efficient, and certifiable performance relative to what the paper establishes.
key_findings.evidence: The tutorial offers useful conceptual connections and small demonstrations, but no new convergence theorem, learned update rule, cross-instance benchmark, matched runtime study, OPF/NNV experiment, or uncertainty analysis. Several central derivations are wrong and several certification claims merely restate strong duality or cite external lossless-relaxation conditions. Thus it is best used as a topic map with equations independently rechecked, not as validated evidence for a new scalable pipeline.

method.core_idea: Organize classical primal-dual optimization, automatic differentiation, differentiable optimization layers, and application examples into one tutorial workflow, using NNLS as the recurring derivation and implementation example.
method.mechanism: Optimization problems are reformulated by conic modeling, penalties, null-space variables, Lagrangian/Fenchel duality, or saddle forms. PDG, ADMM, and PDHG are expressed as tensor programs that can be unrolled, while KKT/implicit equations offer a solver-agnostic backward pass under regularity. CVXPYLayers supplies disciplined parametrized canonicalization and implicit differentiation; PyTorch supplies autodiff and GPU tensor updates. Case studies then map this vocabulary to LP, SOCP, neural verification, wireless rate optimization, a resistive OPF surrogate, and graph-Laplacian regularization.
assumptions: Each reformulated problem is convex, or a cited relaxation is genuinely lossless under conditions satisfied by the instance.
Strong duality and the relevant Slater/constraint-qualification assumptions hold before dual certificates or primal recovery are claimed.
Solution maps are locally single-valued/differentiable and their KKT Jacobians are nonsingular for implicit differentiation.
PDHG step sizes satisfy operator-norm conditions and ADMM subproblems are solvable, although these are not stated in the algorithms.
Projected or reparameterized updates preserve the intended KKT system rather than duplicating constraints.
Graph Laplacians are connected or null spaces are handled explicitly; ordinary inverse notation is not used on singular Laplacians.
Quasi-inverse matrices in the wireless case are nonnegative and irreducible so Perron-Frobenius convexification applies.
Small synthetic instances and solver agreement are adequate demonstrations of claimed scale and accuracy.
The linked repository fills in undefined helpers, data construction, solver settings, and hardware omitted from the PDF.
Automatic differentiation provides useful derivatives at nonsmooth active-set transitions rather than merely a framework-selected subgradient.
Optimizing instance variables with Adam is an informative instance of learning to optimize even without a learned optimizer across instances.
Cited works actually support the surrounding claim; at least two references fail this assumption.

techniques.role: Derives reverse-mode gradients as multipliers of intermediate equality constraints.
Expresses LP, SOCP, ECP, QP, and SDP structure in primal-dual standard forms.
Builds composite saddle formulations and motivates PDHG and proximal maps.
Embeds PDG, ADMM, or PDHG iterations in automatic-differentiation graphs.
Computes solution sensitivities through a local optimality system rather than solver history.
Uses CVXPYLayers to turn parameterized convex programs into differentiable layers.
Attempts to reconstruct primal variables from optimality relations after dual optimization.
Vectorizes blockwise dual NNLS subproblems and global projections in PyTorch.
Transforms a conditional wireless rate region into spectral-radius/exponential-cone constraints.
Replaces a lower norm bound by an auxiliary thrust magnitude under external exactness conditions.
Compares gradients returned by a layer with dual variables or envelope-theorem quantities.

evaluations.setting: One unspecified synthetic NNLS instance over 200 iterations
evaluations.metric: Objective, distance to CVXPY primal/dual solutions, and KKT residual
evaluations.result: Figure 3 visually compares PDG, ADMM, and PDHG, but supplies no dimensions, data-generation rule, step sizes, exact terminal values, seeds, or uncertainty; the printed PDG method is mathematically flawed.
evaluations.baseline: CVXPY reference solution and the three classical first-order methods.

evaluations.setting: Per-instance Adam saddle optimization for NNLS at dimensions from 30-by-20 to 150-by-100
evaluations.metric: Absolute objective-value difference and Euclidean solution distance to CVXPY over 16000 iterations
evaluations.result: Curves generally decrease on a log scale but vary by size; no terminal table, runtime, hardware, instance distribution, or comparison to standard NNLS solvers is reported.

evaluations.metric: Reconstruction loss, KKT residuals, primal agreement, and initial gradient heatmap
evaluations.result: Adam reaches reported loss 2.80e-16 after 300 steps with final KKT residuals around 1e-4; the fitted P is not compared with P_true or tested on new signals.
evaluations.baseline: CVXPYLayer solution before learning and the known x_true.

evaluations.setting: Small Stigler diet example plus random LP sizes through 200-by-500
evaluations.metric: Primal/dual agreement, sensitivity agreement, and runtime
evaluations.result: CVXPY and CVXPYLayers visually agree for three foods; Figure 11 reports a CVXPY/Clarabel runtime curve without error bars or a clearly separated differentiable-layer scaling curve.

evaluations.metric: Optimal rate, recovered power, spectral radii, and dV*/dw versus r*
evaluations.result: CVXPY and CVXPYLayers rate vectors agree visually, one spectral constraint is active at radius 1.0000, and envelope gradients match rates in the plotted example.
evaluations.baseline: CVXPY versus CVXPYLayers under the conditional convexification.

evaluations.result: The paper reports error of order 1e-6 after estimating the null-space scalar with the already-computed CVXPY primal solution, so this is a circular consistency check rather than dual-only recovery.

evaluations.setting: Lossless optimal control, neural-network verification, and resistive OPF case studies
evaluations.metric: No concrete empirical protocol or result table in the reviewed PDF
evaluations.result: These sections give formulations and claimed benefits but do not report executable instances, runtimes, accuracy/certification rates, gradient checks, or comparisons; the OPF dual is structurally invalid as printed.
evaluations.baseline: Prior methods are cited but not experimentally compared.

limitations: The paper is an arXiv tutorial draft with placeholder JACM metadata and impossible submission dates, not the printed version of record its template suggests.
The core Fenchel NNLS derivation omits dual feasibility, the generic PDHG dual has a sign error, and the NNLS PDG algorithm mishandles nonnegativity.
The OPF dual applies G^{-1/2} to a graph Laplacian and offers no valid global-optimality argument for the retained nonconvex constraints.
The LRMP recovery assumes a one-dimensional Laplacian null space without stating connectedness and fits its free scalar using the known target primal solution.
Printed PyTorch snippets depend on undefined variables and helper functions and cannot reproduce the figures standalone.
The work does not learn an optimizer across an instance distribution, despite repeatedly framing per-instance variable optimization as learning to optimize.
No dataset-generation protocol, random seeds, hardware, solver tolerances, complete hyperparameters, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported.
Largest displayed problems are modest and do not support the massive-scale framing.
Several case studies are formulations only; lossless control, NNV, and OPF have no numerical evidence in the PDF.
Lossless convexification and wireless convexification are conditional on external assumptions that are not instantiated or stress-tested.
Implicit differentiation boundaries at nonunique, degenerate, nonsmooth, or active-set-changing optima are acknowledged once but not integrated into claims.
At least two citations are topically unrelated to the claims they are used to support.
No comparison is made with the closest modern differentiable-optimization systems or with the extensive existing surveys as a synthesis baseline.
There is no negative-result or failure-rate study for solver divergence, gradient error, ill-conditioning, infeasibility, or rank deficiency.
failure_modes: Dropping a conjugate-domain or nonnegativity-induced dual constraint produces an apparently smooth but incorrect dual objective and invalid certificates.
Dualizing and projecting the same inequality can converge to a primal solution with the wrong multiplier and nonzero KKT stationarity residual.
PDHG can diverge when tau*sigma*||K||^2 is not controlled; the printed algorithm gives no such guard.
Implicit differentiation can fail or return unstable sensitivities when the KKT Jacobian is singular or the active set changes.
A graph Laplacian inverse or one-scalar null-space parameterization fails for singular or disconnected graphs.
Primal recovery from dual variables can be nonunique, ill-conditioned, or circular if missing null-space information is fitted from the primal target.
Projected primal-dual gradient on a nonconvex OPF surrogate can cycle, reach a non-global stationary point, or violate constraints without a convergence theorem.
A lossless conic relaxation can cease to be exact when its external regularity conditions fail.
Perron-Frobenius rate convexification fails if the quasi-inverse is not nonnegative/irreducible or if the positive-vector conditions do not hold.
Learning a sensing matrix on one signal can memorize that signal through a non-identifiable P and fail on new measurements.
The code examples fail immediately because active-set recovery helpers and stopping quantities are undefined.
Calling autodiff on an absolute value at zero selects one subgradient but does not ensure useful primal-dual dynamics or certification.
Solver agreement on one tiny instance can conceal shared modeling mistakes and says nothing about generality or scale.
reusable_insights: Use one running optimization problem to connect computation-graph adjoints, duality, splitting algorithms, and implicit layers—but unit-test every sign and domain constraint across derivations.
Always retain the condition contributed by an infimum over a cone; it is often the entire dual-feasibility constraint.
Choose exactly one mechanism for a simple constraint in a saddle derivation: primal-domain projection or a dual multiplier, unless a justified split formulation uses both.
State operator-norm step-size conditions beside PDHG pseudocode and constraint qualifications beside duality/certification claims.
Distinguish differentiating an optimizer, learning optimizer parameters across tasks, and merely using autodiff to optimize variables for one instance.
For singular structured matrices, specify the range condition and full null-space basis before claiming primal recovery.
Validate implicit gradients by directional finite differences over many well-conditioned and near-degenerate instances, not one envelope identity.
Treat solver agreement as a correctness smoke test and pair it with residuals, independent formulations, scale sweeps, and reproducible data/hardware details.
Separate the exactness conditions of a convex relaxation from the mechanics of making the relaxed solver differentiable.
Keep tutorial bibliographic templates and references clean because placeholder venues and unrelated citations undermine provenance and technical trust.
open_questions: Can the incorrect NNLS Fenchel dual, PDHG sign, PDG update, OPF dual, and LRMP recovery be repaired consistently in a new revision and in the linked code?
What is actually learned across instances in the proposed framework: step sizes, preconditioners, update maps, problem data, or only per-instance variables?
How do the examples compare in wall time, memory, gradient accuracy, and solution residual with CVXPYLayers, JAXopt-style implicit differentiation, BPQP, FFOLayer, and specialized solvers?
Do repaired PyTorch methods scale past the displayed 150-by-100 or 200-by-500 cases on sparse million-variable problems?
How robust are implicit gradients near nonunique solutions, complementarity changes, singular KKT systems, and ill-conditioned cone programs?
Which lossless-convexification regularity conditions are assumed in the optimal-control example, and can a failing instance be shown?
Under what checkable channel conditions is the wireless quasi-inverse nonnegative, and how often do realistic networks satisfy them?
Can the OPF section be replaced by a valid convex relaxation or a clearly labeled local nonconvex method with convergence diagnostics?
How should disconnected Laplacians and multi-dimensional null spaces be handled in dual-to-primal LRMP recovery?
Can all code snippets become self-contained and reproduce every figure from pinned environments and seeds?
What benchmark would demonstrate optimizer generalization across problem distributions rather than fitting one problem at a time?
Which existing surveys and books leave a genuine gap that this tutorial fills beyond combining their topic lists?

competitive_landscape.title: The Elements of Differentiable Programming
competitive_landscape.relationship: The closest current comprehensive tutorial/book on differentiable programming, spanning autodiff, optimization, probability, implicit differentiation, and program design.
competitive_landscape.difference: Elements v4 is much broader and more systematic about the mathematical/programming foundations and is the source this paper repeatedly leans on. The reviewed tutorial narrows to duality plus first-order cone optimization and supplies application/code sketches, but it does not match Elements' breadth or rigor and contains several equation errors.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to Optimize: A Primer and A Benchmark
competitive_landscape.relationship: A primary survey and reproducible benchmark devoted specifically to learned optimizers for continuous optimization.
competitive_landscape.difference: The JMLR article defines model-based/model-free L2O taxonomies, studies generalization and failure boundaries, and releases Open-L2O benchmarks. The reviewed paper instead mostly implements classical solvers and differentiable layers, with no cross-instance learned-optimizer benchmark; its unique emphasis is pairing cone/Fenchel duality with tutorial case sketches.

competitive_landscape.title: End-to-End Constrained Optimization Learning: A Survey
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct conceptual survey of integrating constrained/combinatorial optimization and machine-learning architectures end to end.
competitive_landscape.difference: Kotary et al. organize learning approaches around feasibility, optimality, solver integration, and structural inference. The reviewed tutorial is more elementary and continuous/conic, includes software walkthroughs and derivations, but does not provide a comparable taxonomy or critical evidence synthesis.

competitive_landscape.title: Differentiable Convex Optimization Layers in Neural Architectures: Foundations and Perspectives
competitive_landscape.relationship: A focused survey on the foundations, evolution, and applications of differentiable convex optimization layers.
competitive_landscape.difference: Katyal centers the neural-architecture optimization-layer literature and its mathematical proofs. The reviewed paper adds classical first-order algorithms, GPU-oriented snippets, duality, and domain examples, but much of its differentiable-layer overview overlaps and its case-study validation is thinner.

competitive_landscape.title: Differentiable Convex Optimization Layers
competitive_landscape.relationship: The foundational CVXPYLayers/DPP primary paper for general differentiable disciplined convex programs used throughout the tutorial.
competitive_landscape.difference: Agrawal et al. contribute ASA canonicalization, analytical cone-solver differentiation, implementations, and timed applications. The reviewed tutorial reuses this machinery in small examples and adds exposition around first-order dual methods, but contributes neither a replacement layer nor a technical extension to DPP.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient and Modular Implicit Differentiation
competitive_landscape.relationship: A primary framework paper for solver-agnostic automatic implicit differentiation through user-specified optimality conditions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Blondel et al. make the implicit-differentiation mechanism modular, benchmark it, and show bilevel applications. The reviewed tutorial gives only the textbook implicit-function formula and delegates implementation to CVXPYLayers, while focusing more on duality and explicit PDG/ADMM/PDHG unrolling.

competitive_landscape.title: BPQP: A Differentiable Convex Optimization Framework for Efficient End-to-End Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A modern differentiable convex-optimization framework that turns the backward pass into a decoupled QP solvable with first-order methods.
competitive_landscape.difference: BPQP provides a concrete new backward algorithm and reports order-of-magnitude runtime improvements on simulated and real tasks. The reviewed paper cites it but neither implements nor benchmarks against it; its claim of efficient first-order differentiable optimization is therefore pedagogical rather than competitive.

competitive_landscape.title: A Fully First-Order Layer for Differentiable Optimization
competitive_landscape.relationship: The closest current method claiming a fully first-order differentiable optimization layer with finite-time hypergradient guarantees and a library.
competitive_landscape.difference: FFOLayer explicitly avoids Hessian/KKT linear solves via an active-set Lagrangian bilevel oracle and gives complexity guarantees. The reviewed tutorial merely notes that classical first-order solvers can be unrolled or embedded; it proposes no first-order hypergradient method and presents no comparison to FFOLayer despite sharing the headline framing.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a unified theoretical tutorial joining differentiable programming, cone programming, Lagrangian and Fenchel-Rockafellar duality, first-order methods, software frameworks, reproducible PyTorch implementations, and diverse LP/SOCP/ECP/QP case studies.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The 44-page draft does place NNLS derivations, PDG/ADMM/PDHG, implicit differentiation, CVXPYLayers, PyTorch snippets, and six domain formulations in one narrative and links a source repository.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novelty is mainly pedagogical packaging. Earlier primary surveys already cover learned optimization and end-to-end constrained optimization; Elements of Differentiable Programming v4 is a broader and more rigorous current tutorial; CVXPYLayers and modular implicit differentiation supply the core machinery; BPQP and FFOLayer make the actual recent algorithmic advances. No new theorem, optimizer, differentiation rule, benchmark, or large-scale empirical result is established here. The synthesis could still be useful as a course note emphasizing duality and case mapping, but the dropped dual constraint, PDHG sign error, invalid PDG, singular-Laplacian OPF dual, circular LRMP recovery, incomplete code, and placeholder publication record materially reduce its technical reliability and make broad efficiency/certification claims non-novel and unsupported.

reviewer_notes: Read all 44 PDF pages of arXiv:2601.16510v4, including all 104 numbered equations, algorithms, code blocks, tables/figures, six case studies, conclusion, and references; this version has no separate appendix or supplement. On 2026-08-23, the exact https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.16510v4 download was byte-compared with the indexed local PDF and matched SHA-256 90d143ca89ed26e759cabc816755d01f0ab252936dfef345ad1f94414923de59; the schema-required locator remains the unversioned indexed export URL. The extraction covers 44/44 pages with no missing-text pages and hashes to 7e3fdee0e8570a65c82c396c7296f9b5d0dece71d1c38d8ffde9d2b52e94b587. Equation audits included scalar counterexamples for the missing NNLS dual constraint and projected/dualized PDG update, plus internal sign, rank, symmetry, null-space, and provenance checks. Current official primary competitors were checked through 2026-08-23 and pinned to exact arXiv revisions or immutable official proceedings/version-of-record identifiers. The linked GitHub repository was not treated as part of the reviewed source, so claims about code refer to the snippets printed in v4.
